blocks.text: Biogeography, the study of the geographic distribution of plants and animals, shows that life in different parts of the world has distinctive evolutionary histories.

items: Similar groups of organisms can live in places separated by vast barriers; their similarities suggest common ancestry and their differences millions of years of independent evolution. For example, the African lion is very similar to the mountain lion of America.

Organisms separated by geographical barriers are often very different despite similar environments; many animals of Australia and Tasmania, where many species of kangaroo are the main herbivores, differ from animals anywhere else.
Islands often have relatively few but unique species, because of colonisation followed by evolution on the island.

blocks.alt: World map centred on the Pacific, with the Equator drawn across it. The range of the African lion is shaded dark red across Africa south of the Sahara and down East Africa; the range of the mountain lion is shaded dark blue down western North America, Central America and most of South America. Picture panels labelled African lion (top left) and Mountain lion (top right) have arrows pointing to the two ranges.
